Reflection and Plane and Curved Mirrors: Light reflects at the same angle as it arrives (angle of incidence = angle of reflection). A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright image the same size and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. A concave mirror converges light, with a focal length f = R / 2, where R is the radius of curvature; a convex mirror diverges light. The mirror equation is 1 / f = 1 / d_o + 1 / d_i, and the magnification is m = -d_i / d_o = h_i / h_o. A positive d_i means a real image and a negative d_i a virtual image; a negative m means an inverted image. Concave mirrors are used in telescopes and makeup mirrors; convex mirrors in vehicle side mirrors for a wide field of view.
Refraction, Lenses and Optical Instrumen: Refraction obeys Snell's law n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2). A converging (convex) lens brings parallel rays to a focus; a diverging (concave) lens spreads them. The thin-lens equation is 1 / f = 1 / d_o + 1 / d_i with magnification m = -d_i / d_o; f is positive for converging lenses and negative for diverging lenses. The power of a lens is P = 1 / f in diopters (f in meters). Two thin lenses in contact have P = P1 + P2. A simple magnifier, a microscope (two converging lenses) and a telescope use lenses to produce larger images or bring distant objects closer. The human eye uses a converging lens to form a real image on the retina; short sight is corrected with a diverging lens and long sight with a converging lens.
Interference and Young's Double Slit: Light waves interfere. In Young's double-slit experiment coherent light passes through two narrow slits separated by a distance d and forms bright and dark fringes on a screen a distance L away. Bright fringes (constructive interference) occur where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths: d sin(theta) = m lambda, m = 0, 1, 2... Dark fringes occur at (m + 1/2) lambda. For small angles the fringe spacing is delta y = lambda L / d. The central bright fringe is at m = 0. Thin films produce colors by interference between light reflected from the front and back surfaces; a phase change of half a wavelength occurs on reflection from a medium with a higher refractive index. Coatings on lenses reduce reflection.
Diffraction, Polarization and Resolution: Diffraction is the spreading of waves around obstacles or through a gap. For a single slit of width a the dark fringes occur at a sin(theta) = m lambda (m = 1, 2, 3...) and the central bright fringe is twice as wide as the others. A diffraction grating with N lines per meter has a slit spacing d = 1 / N and its bright maxima are at d sin(theta) = m lambda, giving sharper and brighter lines used in spectrometers. Polarization shows that light is a transverse wave: polarized light vibrates in one plane. Malus's law gives the intensity through a polarizer, I = I0 cos^2(theta). The Rayleigh criterion says that two sources are just resolved when the angular separation is theta = 1.22 lambda / D for a circular aperture of diameter D; large telescopes resolve better.
Dispersion, Color and the Electromagneti: The refractive index depends slightly on wavelength, so a prism spreads white light into a spectrum: dispersion. Violet light is refracted most and red least in normal materials. Rainbows come from refraction, internal reflection and dispersion in raindrops. The colors we see depend on the light reflected or transmitted: a red object reflects red light and absorbs the rest. Primary colors of light are red, green and blue, and mixing them gives white; pigments subtract colors. Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum, which runs in order of increasing frequency: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. All travel at c = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum and obey c = f lambda. Higher frequency means higher photon energy, E = h f.
